I doubt I'll be able to see anything, but I want an accurate estimate of whether the Moon is visible right now.

I'm in Santiago, Chile at 2026-04-05 06:09 -04 (UTC-0400) (2026-04-05T10:09:00Z in UTC), at latitude -33.4489 degrees and longitude -70.6693 degrees. Based on the data you provided, **yes, you should be able to see the Moon quite clearly.**

Here is the breakdown of why it is highly likely to be visible for you:

### 1. Altitude and Position
The Moon is at an altitude of **48.3 degrees**. In practical terms, this means it is nearly halfway between the horizon and the zenith (the point directly above your head). It is not "hugging" the horizon, where atmospheric haze and buildings usually obscure the view. 

The azimuth of **271.8 degrees** places it almost directly to your **West**. Since it is 10:09 AM UTC (which is 6:09 AM local time in Santiago), the Moon is high in the western sky as the night ends.

### 2. Illumination and Phase
At **89.48% illumination**, the Moon is in its Waxing Gibbous phase, very close to being a Full Moon. Because it is so highly illuminated, it will be very bright. Even if the sky were not perfectly clear, a Moon this bright is difficult to miss.

### 3. Sky Conditions (Nautical Twilight)
You mentioned the sky is in **nautical twilight**. This is the period when the sun is between 6 and 12 degrees below the horizon. During nautical twilight, the horizon is still somewhat visible, but the sky is dark enough that a bright celestial object like a nearly-full Moon will stand out sharply against the blue/grey backdrop.

### 4. Visibility Factors
*   **Atmospheric Clarity:** You noted the sky is clear. In Santiago, while there can be some light pollution or smog, a Moon at a 48-degree altitude is high enough to sit above most of the denser lower-atmosphere interference.
*   **Human Vision:** As an adult with normal unaided eyesight, a Moon that is 89% illuminated is one of the easiest objects in the night sky to spot. It will be significantly brighter than any star or planet.

### Summary
Because the Moon is **high in the western sky**, **nearly full**, and the **sky is clear** during the transition from night to day, you should have no trouble spotting it. You won't need to hunt for it; it should be one of the most prominent objects in the sky.
